chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Crises of the 21st Century

lessons.title: The Eurozone Debt Crisis: Greece and the Limits of a Shared Currency

body.text: A country that shares a currency with its neighbours gives up its three emergency exits: it cannot devalue, it cannot print money, and without a shared budget it cannot count on automatic transfers. When a crisis comes, all the pain lands on wages, jobs and public spending.

children.text: In October 2009, George Papandreou's newly elected Greek government opened the national accounts and announced that the previous numbers had been wrong. Greece's budget deficit for 2009 would not be the figure earlier reported, but 12.7% of GDP. Eurostat later put it at 15.4%. The rules of the eurozone said deficits should stay under 3%.
Within months, investors were asking whether a country using the euro could default. The answer took nine years, three bailouts and the largest sovereign debt restructuring in history to work out.

stats.label: Greek budget deficit, 2009
stats.context: Final Eurostat figure, after repeated revisions

body.caption: The eurozone crisis on the five-stage map

cells: Build-up
After joining the euro, Greece and other southern members borrow at nearly German interest rates, and money flows from the core to the periphery
Trigger
Greece reveals in late 2009 that its deficit is far larger than reported, just as the 2008 crisis has weakened banks and economies
Panic and recognition
Bond yields soar for Greece, then Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy; banks and governments drag each other down
Policy response
EU and IMF bailouts with strict austerity, a 2012 write-down of Greek private debt, and the ECB's "whatever it takes" pledge
Repair and recovery
Years of recession and reform; Greece exits its final bailout programme on 20 August 2018

children.text: The Three Missing Exits
Most crises you have studied so far ended with a currency falling and a central bank acting. The eurozone was different because it is a
monetary union
without a full
fiscal union

markDefs.definition: A group of countries sharing a single currency and a single central bank, which sets one interest rate for all of them.
An arrangement where a central government collects taxes and spends across all regions, automatically transferring money from stronger regions to weaker ones in a downturn.

body.caption: What a country normally uses in a crisis, and what Greece had

cells: Devalue the currency
Yes: the rupee was devalued by about 18% in July 1991
No: Greece used the euro, which it did not control
Own central bank as lender of last resort
Yes: the RBI answers to Indian conditions
No: the ECB sets policy for the whole eurozone
Automatic transfers from a central budget
Not relevant: India was a single country with one budget
Very limited: the EU budget is small, so help came as loans with conditions

children.text: Without the first two tools, Greece could only regain competitiveness through
internal devaluation
. That meant years of falling wages and rising unemployment.

markDefs.definition: Cutting wages, prices and public spending inside a country to make it more competitive, instead of letting the currency fall. It achieves a similar result to devaluation, but slowly and through unemployment.

body.title: Why Not Just Devalue?
body.question: In 1991, India made its exports cheaper by devaluing the rupee. Why could Greece not do the same in 2010?
options: The IMF banned devaluation after the Asian crisis
Greece used the euro, whose value and interest rate were set for the whole eurozone, so it had no national currency to devalue
Greece had already devalued the drachma the year before
Devaluation only works for countries with large oil exports
body.explanation: Greece had replaced the drachma with the euro in 2001. The euro's exchange rate reflects the whole eurozone, including Germany, so Greece could not cut it alone. The only way to make Greek goods cheaper was to cut Greek wages and prices directly, a far slower and more painful process. Leaving the euro to bring back the drachma was discussed in 2015, but it would have meant bank chaos and huge losses on euro debts.

children.text: Build-up: German Interest Rates for Everyone

Before the euro, lenders charged Greece much higher interest rates than Germany, because the drachma could be devalued and Greek inflation was higher. Once Greece joined the euro in 2001, markets treated its bonds as almost as safe as German ones. In early 2007, Greece paid only about 0.25 percentage points more than Germany on 10-year bonds.

Cheap borrowing flowed into government spending in Greece, property booms in Ireland and Spain, and rising wages across the south, while banks in France and Germany lent heavily into those economies. As in Chapter 1's build-up stage, success hid the risk.

body.text: Markets priced Greek bonds as if the rest of the eurozone would always stand behind them. The rules actually said no member was responsible for another's debts. When that assumption was tested, the gap between the two was the crisis.

children.text: Panic: The Doom Loop
The eurozone crisis was driven by a vicious cycle between governments and their banks, often called the
doom loop

markDefs.definition: A self-reinforcing spiral in which banks hold large amounts of their own government's bonds, so a fall in bond prices weakens the banks, and the government's cost of rescuing those banks weakens its finances further.

children.text: Investors start doubting a government's ability to repay, so its bond prices fall.
Domestic banks hold large amounts of those bonds, so their capital shrinks.
Weaker banks cut lending, and the economy shrinks, reducing tax revenue.
The government must rescue its banks or watch them fail, adding to its debt.
Investors doubt the government even more, and the loop repeats.

body.title: A Bank Caught in the Loop
body.prompt: A Greek bank holds €20 billion of Greek government bonds and has €8 billion of capital. In the 2012 restructuring, private holders of Greek bonds took a 53.5% cut in the face value of their bonds. Using that cut, how much in € billion does the bank lose on its Greek bonds?
body.explanation: Loss = €20 billion × 53.5% = €10.7 billion. That is more than the bank's entire €8 billion of capital, so the bank is insolvent. The Greek government, already in crisis, would then have to find money to recapitalise it. That is the doom loop in one calculation.

events.title: Greece's hidden deficit
events.description: The new government reveals a 2009 deficit of 12.7% of GDP, later revised by Eurostat to 15.4%. Public debt is later put at about 127% of GDP for 2009.

events.title: First Greek bailout
events.description: The EU and IMF agree a €110 billion rescue, tied to deep spending cuts and tax rises.

events.title: Ireland needs help
events.description: Its property and banking bust, and a guarantee of its banks' debts, lead to an €85 billion rescue package.

events.title: Portugal follows
events.description: Portugal agrees a €78 billion rescue package.

events.title: The biggest sovereign restructuring in history
events.description: About 97% of privately held Greek bonds, around €197 billion, take a 53.5% cut in face value, reducing Greek debt by about €107 billion. Greek 10-year yields had risen above 40% at the peak of the panic.

events.title: Spain's bank rescue
events.description: Eurozone partners agree up to €100 billion to recapitalise Spanish banks hit by the property bust.

events.title: Whatever it takes
events.description: ECB President Mario Draghi says the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. In September, the ECB announces its Outright Monetary Transactions bond-buying programme.

events.title: Cyprus and the bail-in
events.description: Cyprus receives a €10 billion rescue, and large bank depositors are forced to take losses.

events.title: Greek banks shut
events.description: Capital controls are imposed and cash withdrawals are limited to €60 a day. On 5 July, 61.3% of voters reject the bailout terms in a referendum, but Greece signs a third programme of up to €86 billion in August.

events.title: Greece exits its final bailout
events.description: Nine years after the crisis began, Greece leaves the programme with an economy about a quarter smaller than before.

children.text: The Turning Point: A Lender of Last Resort, Again

Bailouts helped individual countries, but yields kept rising for large economies like Spain and Italy that were too big to rescue country by country. Investors feared a member might leave the euro, which would turn euro debts into a devalued new currency. The panic only broke when the central bank for the whole eurozone stepped in.

On 26 July 2012, Mario Draghi said the ECB was ready to do "whatever it takes" to preserve the euro. In September, the ECB announced Outright Monetary Transactions, a promise to buy the bonds of eurozone governments under stress, provided they agreed to a reform programme. Spreads began falling steadily, even though the programme was never actually used.

body.label: A Promise That Never Had to Be Used
body.context: The credible threat of unlimited central bank support was enough to end the panic. This is Bagehot's rule from Chapter 2 applied to governments: a lender of last resort only needs to be believed, not necessarily to lend.

body.title: Go deeper: the Cyprus bail-in and what it means for depositors

children.text: Until 2013, rescues in Europe were bailouts: governments and taxpayers put money in, and bank depositors were protected. Cyprus broke that pattern.
Cypriot banks had grown far larger than the island's economy and had heavy losses, including on Greek bonds written down in 2012. To limit the size of its €10 billion rescue, Cyprus imposed a
bail-in
. Deposits up to the €100,000 insurance limit were protected, but large depositors above that limit took heavy losses.

markDefs.definition: Making a failing bank's own creditors, such as bondholders and uninsured depositors, absorb its losses by writing down or converting their claims, instead of using taxpayer money.

headers: Who pays for the bank's losses

cells: Bailout
Taxpayers, through government money
UK and US bank rescues in 2008
Bail-in
The bank's own creditors and uninsured depositors
Cyprus, 2013

children.text: For an Indian saver, the lesson is simple. Deposit insurance limits matter. DICGC covers ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, so large balances in a single bank are not fully protected if that bank fails.

body.title: Bailout or Bail-in?
body.textWithBlank: When a failing bank's losses are covered by writing down its bondholders and large depositors instead of using taxpayer money, it is called a bail-___.
body.explanation: A bail-in. Cyprus in 2013 was the landmark case in the eurozone. You will see bail-in logic again in 2023, when Credit Suisse's AT1 bondholders were wiped out.

children.text: Why India Is Not the Eurozone

India is also a large union of very different regions sharing one currency. Maharashtra and Bihar have very different incomes, much like Germany and Greece. So why does India not face a eurozone-style crisis when a state runs into trouble?

body.title: The eurozone vs India as currency unions

columns.label: Eurozone
points: One currency and central bank, but many separate national governments
Small central budget, so help for a struggling member comes as conditional loans
Each country largely bailed out its own banks, feeding the doom loop
No member is legally responsible for another's debts

columns.label: India
points: One currency, one central bank and one central government
Finance Commission shares central taxes with states: 41% of the divisible pool under the 15th and 16th Finance Commissions
The RBI regulates banks nationwide and supervises state borrowing auctions
Weaker states receive larger shares of central funds through the devolution formula

body.title: Could an Indian State Become Greece?
body.scenario: Imagine a heavily indebted Indian state whose debt has climbed well above most other states, with a large share of revenue going on interest. Headlines ask whether it could "become India's Greece".
body.prompt: Using this lesson, explain which Greek-style risks apply and which do not, and what signals you would watch as an investor in that state's bonds (State Development Loans).
body.modelAnswer: What does not apply: first, the state does not face a sovereign currency crisis. Like Greece, it cannot print money, but unlike Greece, it sits inside a fiscal union. The Finance Commission devolves 41% of the divisible pool of central taxes to states, and weaker states receive larger shares by formula, so transfers flow automatically rather than as emergency loans. Second, there is no doom loop with a state-specific banking system, because Indian banks are regulated nationally by the RBI and hold bonds from many states and the Centre. Third, there is no question of the state leaving the rupee. What does apply: a state with high debt and heavy interest costs can still be squeezed, cutting capital spending, delaying payments to contractors and raising its borrowing costs. Markets can demand a higher spread on its State Development Loans than on stronger states' bonds. Signals to watch: the state's debt to its GSDP ratio and whether it keeps rising; interest payments as a share of revenue receipts; the fiscal deficit against the limits set for states; the spread of its SDL yields over central government securities; off-budget borrowing through state-owned companies; and guarantees the state has given to its power utilities or other entities, which can suddenly become its debt. The lesson from Greece is that hidden liabilities and misreported numbers are what turn a slow squeeze into a sudden crisis.

body.title: Warning Signs for Any Country, State or Company Inside a Shared Currency
steps: Is it borrowing at nearly the same rate as far stronger members, despite weaker finances?
Are its deficit and debt numbers audited independently, and have they been revised sharply before?
Do its own banks hold large amounts of its debt, creating a potential doom loop?
Has it lost competitiveness, with wages rising faster than productivity?
Is there a credible central budget or lender of last resort that will support it in a panic?
Does it have guarantees or off-balance-sheet liabilities that could suddenly become its debt?

points: The eurozone is a monetary union without a full fiscal union, so members in crisis could not devalue, print money or count on automatic transfers
After joining the euro, Greece borrowed at close to German rates until late 2009, when its 2009 deficit was revealed to be far higher than reported, eventually 15.4% of GDP
Banks and governments dragged each other down in a doom loop, leading to rescues for Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain's banks and Cyprus
Greece received €289 billion in loans across three programmes, wrote down privately held debt by 53.5% in 2012, and lost about a quarter of its economy
The panic ended when the ECB promised to act as lender of last resort in 2012, and India avoids eurozone-style state crises because it has a fiscal union alongside its single currency

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. The bank exercise and the Indian state scenario are hypothetical illustrations and do not refer to any specific bank or state. Historical figures are drawn from Eurostat, ECB, European Stability Mechanism, IMF and other public sources.
